item.title: For clean windows, just press a button
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
There is good news for those who dread cleaning windows. There are robots out there to take on the tedious and sometimes dangerous task, and do a good job of it. Ask Liang Yu. The 55-year-old resident of Guangzhou, Guangdong province, bought a window-cleaning robot for her 11th-floor apartment. Its performance was so impressive that she bought another one for her mother-in-law. It was a welcome alternative to a chore she once tackled or paid someone to do. To get started, Liang fills the robot's water inlet with solution, plugs in the power cord and secures the robot's safety tether beside the window. Then she presses a button. The device, fitted with two discs covered in cleaning pads, clings to the outside of the window and works its way across the glass. "It's a wonderful invention and checks all my boxes. I can clean the windows whenever I want," said Liang, a businesswoman. Initially, Liang was hesitant to buy the robot due to safety concerns. However, after watching livestream demonstrations, she paid about 1,200 yuan ($180) in a promotional sale last year and got one for herself. According to AVC, a home appliances market consultancy, China's window-cleaning robot market expanded from 480 million yuan in 2020 to 1.7 billion yuan in 2025. Chinese window-cleaning robots are drawing attention abroad as well. On Amazon.com, a Canadian consumer commented that "I don't take pleasure in cleaning, so I really like this robot as it reduces the amount of effort for me. ... Just plop it on a window as you take care of other cleaning tasks". At the recent 140th China Import and Export Fair, or Canton Fair, in Guangzhou, window-cleaning robots made by Chinese companies drew crowds of potential overseas buyers. One such manufacturer is Shanxi Jiashida Robot Technology. Established in 2012, the company exports its products to 56 countries and regions, including the United States, Germany and Japan, with Europe being its main market. Feng Fenfen, head of the company's foreign trade department, said that customers at home and abroad want effective cleaning at a good price, while overseas buyers place more emphasis on safety and environmental protection. The company's product has a dual-disc design, with each disc acting as a suction cup while fitted with a cleaning pad. The discs work alternately, with one holding against the glass while the other moves. Autonomous path-planning technology helps the robot identify edges and adjust its cleaning operation. Feng said the company has adapted its products for different markets. The suction system is adjusted to deal with extreme cold climates, while in areas prone to sand and grit, a dedicated model is designed to remove these particles prior to washing. Niu Liqun, chairman of the company, said the company will keep using real scenarios to drive its technology development. The industry is also moving toward consistent performance benchmarks, with China's first household window-cleaning robots standard set to take effect on Dec 1. It sets unified threshold requirements and criteria. Chinese manufacturers such as Ecovacs and Dreame Technology are also integrating algorithms into their window-cleaning robots. Wei Wei, deputy dean of the School of Computer and Information Technology at Shanxi University, said: "With breakthroughs in multimodal perception, intelligent decision-making and large model technologies, window-cleaning robots are evolving from automated devices into intelligent autonomous machines." For robot users, a chore that once required effort, expense and planning now begins with a button.

item.title: Major changes in US foreign policy 'unlikely'
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
As a decisive blue wave sweeps the United States in the midterm elections, with the Democrats winning clear majorities in both the Senate and the House of Representatives, analysts expect stronger scrutiny of the administration led by US President Donald Trump, but noted that the shift in congressional power may not necessarily effect major changes in the US' foreign policy. As of Wednesday, Democrats and independents who caucus with them had secured at least 54 seats in the 100-member Senate, including traditionally Republican strongholds such as Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, while counting continued in some states. In the 435-member House, Democrats had already won 240 seats to cross the majority threshold, even though some races had not yet been called. The newly elected Congress will be sworn in on Jan 3. In a discussion hosted by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs on Wednesday, Daniel Drezner, a professor at Tufts University in Massachusetts, linked the US' foreign policy and the economic concerns of voters. "Americans fundamentally do not care about foreign policy, unless it affects their bottom line," Drezner said, as the discussion repeatedly veered between the impact of the Iran war and the increasing cost of living. Justin Logan, director of defense and foreign policy studies at the Cato Institute in Washington, DC, wrote on the institute's website on Wednesday that the Iran war played an unusually important electoral role because voters had to bear the brunt of high energy prices. In his first comments on Wednesday after Democrats pulled off a striking election performance, Trump largely agreed with Vice-President JD Vance, who publicly ruminated on the Iran war being a catastrophe for Republicans. "It's largely true because it drove gasoline up a little bit," Trump said, while Vance said in a post on social media that the "real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone". While the newly elected Congress is likely to prepare a vast oversight agenda to rein in the Trump administration, Jack Midgley, an adjunct associate professor at Georgetown University in Washington, DC, told China Daily that the US president's veto power and broad executive authority would limit the Democrats' ability to enact major legislation. Congressional investigations could take precedence over lawmaking, he said. Drezner, from Tufts University, drew a distinction between the Democratic Congress elected in 2006, which failed to prevent then president George W. Bush's troop surge in Iraq, and the Democratic Congress elected in 1974, which built on Watergate-era reforms passed by its predecessor to help sustain and enforce stronger limits on executive power. The professor said that he expects the newly elected Congress to land somewhere between those two precedents. Experts from the Council on Foreign Relations in New York noted that Democrats would chair committees, exercise leverage over federal spending and, through the Senate, decide whether to confirm senior administration nominees. Pierre Yared, a senior fellow at the CFR, said that Democratic control of Congress is unlikely to unilaterally change Trump's tariff policy, because the president is exercising congressionally delegated authority. Drezner, however, indicated the possibility of a bipartisan action, because some Republicans also oppose Trump's tariffs. Meanwhile, fiscal disputes could prove consequential beyond Washington. Josh Lipsky and Bart Piasecki of the Atlantic Council warned in an article published on Wednesday that negotiations on federal spending and the debt ceiling in 2027 could create uncertainty for US financial markets and the global economy. Reflecting on other areas of foreign policy, Christopher Preble, a senior fellow and director at the Stimson Center in Washington, called on lawmakers to use oversight and funding powers to press for an end to the Iran war. Leslie Vinjamuri, president and CEO of the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, said that Trump could pursue diplomatic agreements, including on Ukraine, to build a presidential legacy at this critical juncture of his term, rather than becoming more confrontational abroad. Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia at the CFR, noted that the US' Asian allies could expect and welcome stronger congressional oversight, but they should not expect immediate tariff relief given Trump's veto power. Andrew Hyde, a senior fellow and director at the Stimson Center, warned European governments not to count on Democratic control of Congress bringing back the old transatlantic relationship. For Democrats, gaining control is only the beginning of a tough test. Vinjamuri, from the Chicago Council, said what truly matters to voters is whether the party can help deliver lower food, housing and gasoline prices. Jan Yumul in Hong Kong and Cui Haipei in Dubai, UAE, contributed to this story.

item.title: 9th China International Import Expo opens in Shanghai
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
Despite rising uncertainties and headwinds in global trade, confidence of foreign companies in China remains unchanged, and this can be largely attributed to the country's continued efforts to advance higher-level opening-up and facilitate innovation, officials and top executives attending the 9th China International Import Expo said. That confidence is reflected in the record highs registered at this year's CIIE, which opened in Shanghai on Thursday and runs through Tuesday. Altogether, 4,142 overseas exhibitors are present at this year's business exhibition — the core commercial segment — more than in any previous editions. Furthermore, the total exhibition area exceeds 440,000 square meters for the first time, and more than 480 exhibits are expected to make their debut, another high. In his speech during Thursday's opening ceremony, Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang said that various opening-up policies of China have been first introduced or better interpreted to the world through the CIIE. Quality products, innovative services, frontier technologies and application scenarios have all been extended worldwide through the expo. He said that amid a rapidly changing world economy, the consecutive CIIE editions are China's active moves to advocate an open world economy and strike a dynamic balance in world trade. Alexander De Croo, administrator of the United Nations Development Programme, said that while the world is facing rising pressures due to economic uncertainty, geopolitical tensions and climate change, the CIIE provides a crucial platform of dialogue and cooperation. The value of the CIIE lies not only in opening up the Chinese market, but also in the business ties that are created and tightened in the process, sharpening competitiveness of economies and elevating prosperity, he said. Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker agreed that dialogues addressing challenges and different perspectives openly and constructively form the very foundation of common prosperity. "Europe does not seek isolation. We seek engagement while also ensuring that our economic resilience and industrial capabilities remain strong," said Stocker, advocating deeper China-Austria cooperation in future-oriented technologies. Speaking at Thursday's event, Gabonese President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema applauded China's green transition and digitalization. He said the zero-tariff treatment that China has comprehensively granted since May 1 to African countries that have diplomatic relations with China will help to build a community with a shared future for humanity. This year, the number of Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders attending the CIIE tops 300 for the first time. Caterpillar Inc, a United States-based construction and mining machinery manufacturer, is showcasing a range of digital technologies, energy solutions and services to address challenges across the infrastructure, mining and energy sectors. Alan Yang, the company's senior vice-president, considers the expo a valuable platform to connect with customers and key stakeholders, better understand their evolving needs and explore new opportunities. This year's expo is hosting over 2,000 first-time exhibitors, including Singapore-based Perennial Holdings. The group's project in Tianjin — China's first wholly foreign-owned tertiary comprehensive hospital — began operations in February 2025. A similar project is expected to open in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, at the end of this year, according to Zhai Lili, the company's head for brand promotion in China. Such progress testifies to China's institutional opening-up in trade of services, she said. Around 170 enterprises and 30 overseas organizations have participated in all nine editions of the CIIE. Swedish medical technology company Elekta is one of them. Gong Anming, president for China at Elekta, said the company is shifting from introducing global technologies to developing innovations locally and bringing Chinese clinical experience to international markets.

item.title: Live: Protests sweep Europe
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
European law enforcement agencies have vowed to throw the full weight of the law at cost-of-living protesters after demonstrations across the continent spread and turned violent. Calls for gatherings on social media prompted police to step up security in several cities. Public services, the cost of living and housing affordability remained key concerns in many of the protests. A weekend cyberattack on refrigeration systems at French blood storage facilities attempted to raise temperatures to potentially dangerous levels, authorities disclosed on Wednesday. Three cold storage sites operated by the French Blood Establishment, or EFS, in the Burgundy-Franche-Comte region of east-central France, were affected after hackers breached systems run by Coolworld, a Dutch refrigeration and remote monitoring provider. The attack was first reported on Wednesday by Le Canard Enchaine, a French weekly newspaper, which said temperature settings on units storing plasma and blood samples were reprogrammed from around -30 C to 110 C — well above boiling point. Officials stressed these were target settings entered into the system, not actual temperatures reached inside storage rooms. Workers averted disaster after a night-shift technician spotted the anomaly and moved quickly to transfer or secure affected products. EFS President Frederic Pacoud said the attack could have resulted in the loss of plasma destined for patients, but a warning system ensured "there was no compromise to the safety of blood products". No health consequences or product losses were reported, and distribution operations continued uninterrupted, an EFS statement said. "Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing employees to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised," it added. Authorities have since disabled remote access to the compromised units. The Health Ministry credited monitoring and alarm systems with protecting blood supplies from damage. On Wednesday, Coolworld acknowledged the incident, saying it had "responded promptly by implementing the appropriate measures". The company attributed the security flaw to third-party software. "The vulnerability currently being reported in the media concerns a component supplied by a third-party provider and not directly controlled by Coolworld," it said. Operations across five countries — France, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom — fall under Coolworld's remit. Investigators from France's national cybersecurity agency and Health Ministry are probing the breach, but said no suspects have been identified. Similar intrusions struck refrigeration infrastructure elsewhere across Europe last month. Freezers and refrigerators were compromised at supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium, and the Netherlands in mid-October, spoiling large quantities of food. Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch retail giant hit in that wave, warned Wednesday the damage could cut fourth-quarter sales by up to $281 million and reduce operating income by more than $112 million. "While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations," the retailer's CEO Frans Muller said. In the United States, Pentagon officials are investigating cyberattacks in August that hit food storage coolers at several military bases, destroying an undisclosed amount of supplies. PARIS -- Around 600,000 people took part in demonstrations across France on Thursday, French television channel BFM TV reported, citing an initial estimate by the French Interior Ministry. However, the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) estimated that nearly 1.6 million people took part in Thursday's demonstrations nationwide, including 350,000 in Paris, according to BFM TV. According to figures released by the French Ministry of National Education, 16 percent of teachers were on strike on Thursday. Meanwhile, nearly 33 percent of higher education institutions were disrupted by the movement as of midday, affecting 60 of the country's 184 institutions. Nearly 10 percent of employees in the French state civil service took part in Thursday's strike over salaries and purchasing power, according to figures released by the Ministry of Public Action and Accounts. Transport services were generally maintained, French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said in a post on social media platform X, adding that as of 2 pm (1300 GMT), nine out of 10 high-speed TGV trains were operating, along with about two-thirds of regional trains. The latest mobilization followed several rounds of protests in France since September, initially led by students demanding better educational conditions before spreading to the streets and drawing in other groups. On Oct 17, around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations across France, bringing together farmers, climate activists, trade unions and students. Their demands covered fuel prices, the cost of living, education and public services. PARIS -- The Eiffel Tower was closed to visitors on Thursday due to a nationwide strike in France, as demonstrations also took place across the country. "Due to the nationwide strike, the Eiffel Tower is closed today," the landmark's official website announced. By 1 pm local time (1200 GMT), 270,000 demonstrators had been reported at 180 demonstrations across France, excluding Paris, French television channel BFM TV reported, citing sources close to the interior minister. According to figures released by the French Ministry of National Education, 15.81 percent of teachers were on strike on Thursday, BFM TV reported. Meanwhile, nearly 33 percent of higher education institutions were disrupted by the movement as of midday, affecting 60 of the country's 184 institutions. BELGRADE - Serbian authorities detained nine active police officers and one former officer on Wednesday for allegedly using excessive force against detainees during anti-corruption protests last year in Belgrade, the country's Interior Ministry said. Anti-corruption protests swept across Serbia, a candidate for European Union membership, in 2025 and 2026 after 16 people died when a concrete canopy on a renovated railway station in the city of Novi Sad collapsed on Nov 1, 2024. The protests ultimately resulted in the ouster of the populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is loyal to ex-President Aleksandar Vucic, in an Oct 25 snap parliamentary election by the leaderless Student List. The ministry said in a statement that the suspects, who served in an elite unit, tortured and intimidated several persons detained in the garage of the government compound in downtown Belgrade on Aug 14-15, 2025. "By the use of force and threats, (they) inflicted great pain and severe suffering on a larger number of ... persons, intending to obtain information from them and intimidating and unlawfully punishing them," the statement said. The ministry provided only the initials of the officers and former officer who were detained. The news marked the first major arrests in connection with violence against the protesters who took to the streets over the past two years. Police used tear gas, crowd-control vehicles and stun grenades to disperse crowds during the protests. Dozens of students and activists who took part in the protests accused police of excessive use of force that resulted in injuries and psychological trauma. Serbian students, activists, opposition politicians and rights watchdogs have accused Vucic and the SNS of political violence, pressure against media, ties to organised crime and rampant corruption. Vucic and his allies deny the accusations. Reuters LYON/PARIS - French riot police fired tear gas and charged a group of protesters in the French city of Lyon on Thursday as demonstrations took place across the country in a renewed challenge to President Emmanuel Macron after weeks of unrest. Some of the protesters were seen shouting anti-police slogans and some were dressed all in black, with face coverings. The Interior Ministry said police in Lyon had been confronted by several hundred hardcore protesters and that the violence had been contained although tensions remained high. The nationwide protests and a strike by public workers, called by trade unions and backed by student groups, come after demonstrations over living costs, public services and education triggered the worst civil unrest France has seen in years. The unrest comes only five months before a presidential election which could pit far-right candidate Marine Le Pen against hard-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon in a second-round run-off. Macron, who is serving his second term and is unpopular, cannot run again. SCHOOL ABLAZE AFTER FIREWORKS ARE HURLED The Interior Ministry said people throwing fireworks had caused a fire at a high school near the city of Toulouse in the southwest on Thursday morning, forcing pupils and staff to evacuate the building while firefighters doused the flames. "This criminal behaviour is an absolute scandal," said Education Minister Edouard Geffray on X. French high school students and other demonstrators had earlier faced off against riot police in Paris as they blocked a street with rubbish bins on Thursday morning. While the demonstrations in Lyon and other cities including Marseille and Nantes began in the morning, the main protest in Paris was only scheduled to start at 2 pm (1300 GMT), from Place de la Republique. The Eiffel Tower was shut on Thursday because of the strike. "The government tried to block the demonstrations. The demonstrations are bigger than ever," Sophie Binet, head of the CGT trade union, told reporters. She estimated that some 250,000 people were demonstrating across France. "High school students, pensioners, students, workers, all together. Unity wins," read one banner at the protest in Lyon. POLICE DEPLOY IN LARGE NUMBERS "Our pay has not kept up with inflation," said Mehdi Dumontroty, a 45-year-old firefighter who was joining the protest in Paris. "What happened this summer proves that we were right when we said we needed more resources to deal with the crisis that we faced," he said, referring to wildfires caused earlier this year by intense heat waves. Authorities had sought to lower tensions after riots and looting on Oct 17 caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops and public buildings across the country and fuelling criticism of Macron's handling of the crisis. Around 70,000 police were on duty nationwide, a comparable figure to recent weekends. The French government has defended police tactics while saying any abuses would be investigated. The strike contributed to a reduction in France's nuclear output early on Thursday. However, no major problems were reported on the transport network. The Education Ministry said just over 15 percent of French teaching staff had joined the strike. A group of people, some wearing helmets, attacked a student assembly at the University of Athens campus on Wednesday, injuring three people, Greece's medical emergency service and the semi-state Athens News Agency said. The three were treated at an Athens hospital for injuries which were not critical, the emergency service said. Police were investigating the incident. It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack or why. No arrests were immediately reported. The Greek Education Ministry condemned the violence, saying it "insulted the academic community and undermined freedom of expression." Thousands of students and teachers took to the streets across Greece last month, demanding higher state funding for education, better facilities and less-crowded classrooms, echoing protesters in other European countries. Student groups have planned further demonstrations this month. Cities across the Czech Republic saw mass protests on Tuesday because of government plans to alter the funding of the country's public broadcasting network. The government, headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis, recently introduced a parliamentary bill that seeks to cancel the monthly fee of 205 Czech koruna ($9.48) paid by each household to fund the public broadcasting service, bringing an abrupt end to the debate over the issue, and causing a rushed vote. Jakub Szanto, a reporter for the Czech TV channel, told Agence-France Presse the attempt to force the bill through without a proper debate was a "radical step", and added "we firmly hope the government will understand that when something's working, you don't have to change it". In an unprecedented move, workers at public radio and television services joined the protest, with only repeated programs and shorter news bulletins broadcast, and a message on screen saying: "We are doing everything we can to ensure that we can continue to provide a public service in its full scope and quality in the future." Critics of the government's proposal, which would result in a funding cut of around 15 percent, say it is an attempt to limit the independence of the trusted public broadcasting service. "This proposal, if passed, will give the government coalition tools to politically influence the content of both public media," said strike committee member Jan Molacek. Babis, however, insists there is no political agenda and it is purely down to a matter of financing. "None of what the people are protesting against ... is true," he said. OSLO -- About 40,000 high school students across Denmark walked out of classes Wednesday to protest government plans to cut student grants, organizers said. The Danish student organization DGS said students at 57 high schools suspended classes, according to Danish news agency Ritzau. In Copenhagen, protesters gathered at City Hall Square before marching to Christiansborg, the seat of parliament, carrying banners calling for student support to be preserved. DGS and 20 other education and political youth organizations organized the demonstration. The government's proposal would remove grants for students living with their parents whose combined parental income exceeds a specified threshold, and reduce payments for some others. The proposed cuts form part of its budget negotiations. Christina Egelund, minister for Science, Higher Education and Digital Affairs, said she understood students demonstrating for their views, but defended the need to make spending choices amid growing demands for defense and security funding. The grant proposal remained under negotiation, she said. PRAGUE -- Thousands of protesters, including university students and artists, took to the streets in Prague and other cities on Tuesday as Czech public television and radio workers held a one-day strike against a government plan to cut financing and move funding to the state budget. Workers and demonstrators called the plan an attempt to hurt the broadcasters' independence and viability, and they demanded that the government scrap the planned reform. The strike also led to broadcast curbs. The strike escalates a fight over the future of the broadcasters that a 2025 Reuters Institute survey found were among the country's most followed and most trusted news sources. The government's bill passed a preliminary vote last month and now awaits further debate in parliament. Czech Television's 24-hour news broadcast showed a darkened newsroom and moderators dressed in black reading, unusually, from a script. The government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, backed by the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) and eurosceptic Motorists parties, has frequently accused private and public media of bias. The coalition wants to cancel a 205-crown ($9.43) monthly household broadcasting fee — currently used for funding — in its overhaul. Opposition parties have compared the proposed changes to reforms in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, a Babis ally who built an array of pro-government media during his 16 years in office. "This proposal, if passed, will give the government coalition tools to politically influence the content of both public media," Czech TV reporter Jan Molacek, a member of the strike committee, said. The government parties introduced the bill unexpectedly on a Friday last month, curbing debate and forcing a preliminary vote before dawn on the Saturday. On Tuesday, media workers and supporters marched from the Czech Television headquarters to Prague's Wenceslas Square, where thousands gathered to back their demands. "I want the media to continue to be free," said student Alena Jechova, 23. CHANGES POSSIBLE IN FURTHER DEBATE Critics say the funding shift to the budget would remove the relationship between the media and paying viewers, and funding decisions would become open to political pressure. A 15 percent financing cut proposed as part of the change would reduce public television's nominal budget to the level of 2008 and radio's to that of 2005. The media have called such cuts unbearable. Babis reiterated on Monday that the government was merely meeting a promise to lighten the financial burden on the public. "There is no fight over democracy. Nobody wants to take over the public media or bring them under state control," he said, adding that changes to the bill could be made in further debate. Molacek said a funding change was not impossible but needed to be based on a thorough debate and backed by legal safeguards against meddling. PARIS - French high school student protests resumed on Monday on a much smaller scale than in past weeks as pupils returned from a two-week break, with youngsters trying to blockade a few high schools in Paris, Marseille and Rennes, French media reported. By 0830 GMT some 41 high schools — about 1percent of those nationwide — were blockaded, the Education Ministry said. Hundreds of France's more than 3,000 high schools were blockaded in the weeks prior to the break. The protests, which began in the Paris suburbs in September, have spread across France and broadened beyond education to focus on the cost of living, drawing in trade unionists and activists and sometimes turning violent. A wave of so-called "Gen Z" protests has swept across European countries including Germany, Italy, Belgium and Albania, driven by grievances including the cost of living, the poor state of schools and perceived corruption. Last month French protests degenerated into violent clashes with the police and outright riots in several cities, with shops looted, in a test for President Emmanuel Macron's minority government. "In terms of blockades — or rather, attempted blockades — the phenomenon is very marginal. We're talking about just a handful of units, a few individual schools," Education Minister Edouard Geffray told radio station France Inter on Monday morning. He said protests are allowed but preventing access to schools is illegal. Police officers were present, TV footage showed, though not in full anti-riot gear. Students want the renovation of aging schools, more teachers, more university places and the end of a university admissions system they see as socially unfair. Geffray offered last week to cap class sizes at 28, dedicate 4 billion euros ($4.47 billion) to renovating schools, create 15,000 new places for students in higher education and a new admission system by 2028. High school student representatives said the offers were not enough and they would keep protesting. MADRID - Spanish police removed remaining protesters and tents from Madrid's main square early on Tuesday, officials said, after most of the people demonstrating against soaring rents, home shortages and evictions had already left voluntarily. The pre-dawn operation ended a five-week encampment in the Puerta del Sol square that had become a symbol of Spain's housing crisis and contributed to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's decision to call a snap general election for Nov 29. The protests were sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, who later died, with marches called by tenants' unions held across Spain. Similar camps sprang up in squares in other major Spanish cities, as well as in neighbouring Portugal. The one in Sol grew into a miniature city, with its own named "streets", information stands, cultural activities and food distribution. Riot police moved in to clear the camp of its remaining 334 occupants at around 3 am (0200 GMT) on Tuesday and made two arrests for disobedience and resisting officers, the office of the central government's representative in Madrid said in a statement. The operation involved some 400 police, along with firefighters and social services, it said. Protesters said on their Telegram messaging channel that the clearing of the camp had been violent and that several campers were injured after being beaten and attacked with pepper spray. The government said in a separate statement that there had been no violence or disturbances. Reuters footage showed city workers cleaning the square with water hoses, scrubbing graffiti from statues and disposing of the large plastic tarps strung between lamp posts. On Oct 30, the campers' main representatives said they were dissolving their organising committees as their original demand had been met after the government passed several housing measures. Instead, they planned to focus on a general strike over housing rights and cost of living called for Nov 11. According to the government, a large number of the people still sleeping there were homeless or belonged to other vulnerable groups. Agencies The clampdown follows weeks of unrest that began in France as student opposition to education underfunding. The rallies morphed into continentwide mobilizations against cost-of-living increases, a lack of affordable housing, pension privatization, poor public services and several other issues. After protesters in France allegedly hurled incendiaries at police on Saturday, prosecutors there say they have launched an attempted murder investigation and intend to put those responsible behind bars. Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez backed the move, saying anyone who throws an incendiary device at a police officer has carried out "what I call a murder attempt". A police officer who sustained burns to his ankle in the incident told Le Figaro newspaper that he and other officers "suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well-equipped adversaries", who used a "particularly sophisticated" type of incendiary device, with a liquid that "had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail". "We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters," he added. Fourteen other police officers were injured during the weekend protests in France, which were largely peaceful and involved hundreds of thousands of people taking part without resorting to violence or looting. Officers made more than 770 arrests across France over the weekend, which was significantly fewer than has been recorded in recent weeks. Protests also took place in other countries, including Germany, which had previously been relatively calm. Ministers there said they are planning a crackdown after looters and rioters damaged stores and injured more than 100 police officers in a major incident in Frankfurt over the weekend. Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, said more than 1,300 police officers had struggled to maintain order, arresting 54 people aged between 13 and 29. "I was shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugarcoating it," he said. "Things cannot go on like this." Germany has become the latest country in Europe to witness urban unrest after cost-of-living protests on the weekend turned violent. Unrest across continental Europe shows no sign of easing and continues to spread. Protests also took place in France, Italy, Portugal and Spain over rising living costs, housing and education. Some protests involved violent clashes, and hundreds were arrested. (Video Yang Yi) GENEVA -- A protest involving several hundred people turned violent in Zurich, Switzerland on Saturday night, leading to the arrest of two men, Swiss police said in a statement on Sunday. The protesters, some wearing masks, protective goggles or Halloween-style outfits, gathered at a square in District 4 of Switzerland's largest city and mingled with partygoers on Saturday night. The protest turned violent as some protesters set fire to rubbish bins, e-bikes and e-scooters at various locations, the statement said. A car was also set alight, and windows at a public transport stop and several shops were damaged. Police said they came under repeated attacks from protesters throwing fireworks, bottles and stones, and responded by deploying water cannons, tear gas and rubber bullets. Two young Swiss men carrying weapons were arrested when collecting objects at a construction site suspected to be used as projectiles against police, a separate police statement said. According to police, a demonstration also took place in Basel on Saturday evening. Around 150 people marched through the city center, disrupting traffic. Demonstrators erected barricades and set them on fire, while isolated incidents of property damage were reported along the route. According to Swiss media reports, the protests in Zurich and Basel were held under the slogan "We've had enough -- in Switzerland too," with demonstrators drawing parallels with youth protests in France and other European countries. MADRID — Another wave of protests swept across major European cities on Saturday, with demonstrators voicing grievances over issues ranging from living conditions to disputes involving public institutions. Meanwhile, calls for gatherings on social media prompted police to step up security in several cities. In France, around 320,000 people took part in a new round of protests on Saturday, including about 70,000 in Paris, according to the Interior Ministry. Organizers put the nationwide turnout at nearly 500,000, including 200,000 in the capital. Around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed nationwide. Most marches passed off peacefully, though clashes with police and other disturbances were reported in several cities. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters that, according to a preliminary tally, 422 people had been arrested across France. In Germany, demonstrations took place in more than 30 cities on Saturday. Protesters called for greater investment in public services and measures to address the rising cost of living, and opposed compulsory military service. By late afternoon, organizers reported more than 68,000 participants, based on figures from 12 cities. The demonstrations were also largely peaceful, but clashes broke out in several cities in the evening. German news agency dpa reported that police officers were injured in Frankfurt, barricades were set ablaze in Hamburg, and officers came under attack in Bremen. In Portugal, housing protests drew more than 1,000 people each in Lisbon and Porto on Saturday. In Lisbon, demonstrators marched toward Rossio Square, where they planned to camp overnight. Police had dispersed protest encampments in both cities on Oct 25. Political grievances also dominated protests in various countries. In Poland, an escalating dispute over the composition and leadership of the Constitutional Tribunal brought demonstrators onto the streets of Warsaw. Protesters gathered outside the tribunal from Friday evening into Saturday, with police reporting that four people were detained during overnight operations around the building, local media reported. Polish President Karol Nawrocki returned early from a foreign trip and announced urgent political consultations. In Albania, protests demanding better education, improved living conditions and Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation continued for a 19th consecutive day in Tirana on Saturday, according to the Albanian Telegraphic Agency. Some protesters threw stones and Molotov cocktails at the police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons. The opposition Democratic Party backed the movement. Elsewhere, social media calls for gatherings prompted heightened security measures. In the Netherlands, police dispersed a crowd near The Hague Central Station on Saturday afternoon and urged the public to avoid the city center. Local police reported 34 arrests during the day. The gathering followed online calls for demonstrations in several Dutch cities, some of which encouraged looting and vandalism. Some businesses boarded up their storefronts ahead of the planned gatherings. In Spain, police stepped up security in cities including Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia on Saturday following online calls for gatherings, local media reported. The deployments aimed to prevent a repeat of the previous weekend's unrest in Barcelona, which left 15 officers injured and led to 128 arrests. Spanish news agency EFE reported on Friday that police had arrested 10 people nationwide on suspicion of inciting unrest and violence through online channels. XINHUA-AGENCIES Germany has become the latest country in Europe to witness scenes of urban unrest after cost-of-living protests on Saturday turned violent. Largely peaceful demonstrations organized by a group called Gen Z regelt, meaning "Gen Z takes charge", took place in cities including Hamburg, Cologne, Berlin and the country's financial center, Frankfurt, focusing on issues such as public spending cuts and underfunding in schools, the same issue that was the starting point for major disturbances in France in recent weeks. A large area of Frankfurt's main shopping district was closed off overnight by police after premises were looted, and across the country there were reports of water cannons being used to disperse people who were pelting emergency workers with missiles. Roman Poseck, the interior minister of Hesse state, where Frankfurt is situated, said it was "shameful" how the protests had ended, and that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated them. "We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers," he said. "France must not be held up as a model in this regard." Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told newspaper Bild that the actions of police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris", and vowed that troublemakers would receive "harsh punishments". Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems … we are against compulsory military service and we are in favor of a fairer distribution of the burden." France also saw more widespread protests on Saturday, with organizers estimating half a million people turned out, and the authorities saying around 320,000, but compared to the destruction witnessed in recent weeks, the latest demonstrations were largely peaceful. Police had come in for heavy criticism for losing control of previous protests, which degenerated into violence and looting, and prompted French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez to tender his resignation, which was rejected. "Security forces held their ground and protected city centers," he said on Saturday night. "Public order was maintained." The tension in France has an added political dimension, as the country begins its build-up to the presidential election taking place in six months' time. This week, incumbent President Emmanuel Macron, who by law is not allowed to seek a third consecutive term of office, said it was "not normal" for the country to be in such a state of "turmoil" with an election on the horizon. The current wave of protests emerged from teachers going on strike over school funding, with students coming out in support, and Le Monde newspaper quoted student union spokeswoman Sabrine Kharbach as saying "Starting this Tuesday, we will blockade our universities and high schools, and we will do so again on Thursday before joining the demonstration on Nov 5 called by workers and trade unions". PARIS -- A total of 779 people were arrested across France during a new round of protests on Saturday against the rising cost of living, French television channel BFM TV reported Sunday, citing figures from the French Interior Ministry. Around 320,000 people took part in a new round of protests across France on Saturday, according to the ministry. In Paris, the ministry put the number of demonstrators at 70,000 as of 5 pm (1600 GMT) on Saturday. Although most marches passed off peacefully, the dispersal of protesters led to tensions in several cities. In Paris, a homemade explosive device detonated at the feet of a member of the security forces near Porte de Charenton in the 12th arrondissement on Saturday, leaving him slightly injured. The Paris prosecutor's office said Sunday that an investigation had been opened on suspicion of attempted murder in connection with the incident. MADRID -- Another wave of protests swept across major European cities on Saturday, with demonstrators voicing grievances over issues ranging from living conditions to disputes involving public institutions. Meanwhile, calls for gatherings on social media prompted police to step up security in several cities. Public services, the cost of living and housing affordability remained key concerns in many of the protests. In France, around 320,000 people took part in a new round of protests on Saturday, including about 70,000 in Paris, according to Interior Ministry figures. Organizers put the nationwide turnout at nearly 500,000, including 200,000 in the capital. Around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed nationwide. Most marches passed off peacefully, although clashes with police and other disturbances were reported in several cities. French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters that, according to a preliminary tally, 422 people had been arrested nationwide. In Germany, demonstrations took place in more than 30 cities on Saturday. Protesters called for greater investment in public services, measures to address the rising cost of living, and opposed compulsory military service. By late afternoon, organizers reported more than 68,000 participants, based on figures from 12 cities. As in France, the demonstrations in Germany were largely peaceful, but clashes broke out in several cities in the evening. German news agency dpa reported that police officers were injured in Frankfurt, barricades were set ablaze in Hamburg, and officers came under attack in Bremen. In Italy, protesters remained camped near Rome's Colosseum on Saturday following nationwide demonstrations over living costs and public services. Workers and other groups had joined rallies in more than 60 cities on Friday during a general strike called by Unione Sindacale di Base (USB), Italian news agency ANSA reported. The union estimated 1.5 million people took part, while the Interior Ministry put the figure at about 255,000. In Portugal, housing protests drew more than 1,000 people each in Lisbon and Porto on Saturday. In Lisbon, demonstrators marched toward Rossio Square, where they planned to camp overnight. Police had dispersed protest encampments in both cities on Oct 25. Political grievances also dominated protests in various countries. In Albania, protests demanding better education, improved living conditions and Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation continued for a 19th consecutive day in Tirana on Saturday, according to the Albanian Telegraphic Agency. Some protesters threw stones and Molotov cocktails at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons. The opposition Democratic Party backed the movement. In Poland, an escalating dispute over the composition and leadership of the Constitutional Tribunal brought demonstrators onto the streets of Warsaw. Protestors gathered outside Warsaw's Constitutional Tribunal from Friday evening into Saturday, with police reporting four detained during overnight operations around the building, local media reported. Polish President Karol Nawrocki returned early from a foreign trip and announced urgent political consultations. Elsewhere, social media calls for gatherings prompted heightened security measures. In the Netherlands, police dispersed a crowd near The Hague Central Station on Saturday afternoon and urged the public to avoid the city center. Local police reported 34 arrests during the day. The deployments aimed to prevent a repeat of the previous weekend's unrest in Barcelona, which left 15 officers injured and led to 128 arrests. Spanish news agency EFE reported on Friday that police had arrested 10 people nationwide on suspicion of inciting unrest and violence through online channels. WARSAW - Protesters clashed with police outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw on Friday night after the court's president was suspended amid an escalating dispute between Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government and the opposition over control of the judiciary. Police detained three protesters who entered the court's premises. Several people were reportedly injured, according to local media. Hundreds of demonstrators, including supporters of the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, gathered outside the tribunal, accusing Tusk's government of attempting to seize control of the court. PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki were among those present. The confrontation followed months of disputes over judicial appointments. Poland's parliament, where Tusk's ruling coalition holds a majority, has elected eight judges to the tribunal this year. However, President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of the opposition PiS party, accepted the oaths of office of only three. The remaining five took their oaths at parliamentary ceremonies, but Nawrocki and the tribunal's president refused to recognize their status, preventing them from taking up their judicial duties. On Friday evening, the tribunal's website announced that its president and vice president had been suspended for one month, with a newly elected judge whose status remains disputed assuming temporary leadership. The tribunal's leadership rejected the move, accusing those involved of illegally taking over its website and describing the action as a "coup." Nawrocki cut short his trip to Senegal and returned to Poland, where he held an emergency meeting with judicial officials late Friday. Shortly after midnight, he visited the Constitutional Tribunal and entered the court building.

item.title: US companies' presence at CIIE expands
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
Companies from the United States are expanding their presence at China's flagship import expo, underscoring China's enduring appeal as a consumer market and manufacturing hub amid an evolving global trade and investment landscape. From agricultural products and advanced manufacturing technologies, to innovative industrial goods and logistics solutions, US companies including Archer-Daniels-Midland, Rockwell Automation, 3M and FedEx are showcasing their latest offerings at the 9th China International Import Expo, which runs from Thursday to Tuesday in Shanghai. Senior executives from those companies said that China's vast market, industrial upgrading and growing demand for innovation continue to create opportunities for US businesses. US exhibitors have secured more than 50,000 square meters of exhibition space at the CIIE this year, an increase of 1,500 square meters from last year, according to the Ministry of Commerce. The US has ranked first among participating countries and regions by exhibition area for eight consecutive years. ADM, the Chicago, Illinois-based agribusiness group and a seven-time CIIE participant, plans to sign agreements worth 32 billion yuan ($4.8 billion) with customers and industry partners for soybean and grain imports at this year's expo. Quan Ping, president of ADM China, said the CIIE provides an opportunity to better understand customer needs, deepen industry partnerships and turn global expertise into practical solutions tailored to the Chinese market. "We aim to combine our global capabilities with local market insights to create greater value for customers and partners, while bringing more innovative products and solutions to China," Quan said. Rockwell Automation, which is exhibiting at the CIIE for the sixth consecutive year, is showcasing new automation controllers and smart manufacturing solutions as the US company seeks to tap into China's growing demand for industrial artificial intelligence and more efficient production systems. Ian Shih, president of Rockwell Automation (China), said his company sees opportunities in China's intelligent equipment, new energy, life sciences, advanced manufacturing and industrial digitalization sectors, driven by growing demand for smarter and more flexible production systems. Fu Suixin, an associate researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of American Studies, said that US multinationals increasingly see China as more than a sales market, given its role in global innovation and supply chains and the deep economic ties between the two countries. Investment momentum The continued interest is also reflected in investment flows. China's actual use of foreign investment from the US rose 7.7 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, while more than 6,300 foreign-invested companies made additional investments in China, data from the Ministry of Commerce showed. US industrial group 3M, which has never missed an edition of the CIIE, is showcasing its latest technologies and products in automotive, electronics, safety, manufacturing materials and automation, with several products making their global or China debuts. "We have always viewed the CIIE as a key trade fair for showcasing cutting-edge innovations and expanding local partnerships," said Henry Ding, president of 3M China. He added that 3M and Chinese sportswear company Anta Sports Products will sign a memorandum of understanding at the event to establish a joint innovation laboratory focused on applications of sustainable materials in outdoor sports. US express transportation company FedEx is showcasing solutions in smart logistics, sustainable operations and specialized transportation services this year at the CIIE. Poh-Yian Koh, president of FedEx China, said that as AI, digitalization and evolving supply chains reshape global commerce, Chinese businesses need more than transportation. They require trusted partners that can provide the connectivity, visibility and resilience needed to expand globally. Wu Di, deputy head of the department of foreign investment administration at the Ministry of Commerce, said China will expand opening-up trials in cloud computing, biotechnology and wholly foreign-owned hospitals, and create new opportunities in emerging industries and digital and low-carbon development.

item.title: CIIE demonstrates potential of Chinese market
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
There is a selective myopia in the way some in the West discuss China, focusing too sharply on its export capabilities while overlooking what the world's second-largest economy imports and the opportunities its vast market offers foreign businesses. As protectionism and unilateralism disrupt the global trading system, the ninth China International Import Expo, opening in Shanghai on Thursday, offers a useful corrective lens for this shortsightedness. Since its inception in 2018 as the world's first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports, the CIIE has evolved into an international public good: a platform through which businesses, economies and developing countries can gain access to China's development opportunities. This year's event has attracted 4,142 overseas exhibitors from 148 countries and regions, including more than 2,000 first-time participants. That is hardly the profile of a market "taking advantage of" others. The persistence of the so-called "China Shock" narrative rests on an inversion. China's manufacturing competitiveness is falsely presented as a "threat", while the benefits of its enormous market, comprehensive industrial ecosystem and growing demand are routinely pushed into the background. The result is a political construct that turns economic interdependence into a zero-sum contest. The facts tell a different story. China's foreign trade in goods reached 39.94 trillion yuan ($5.94 trillion) in the first three quarters of 2026, up 18.8 percent year-on-year. More tellingly, imports grew by 22.3 percent to 16.74 trillion yuan, outpacing the 16.4 percent increase in exports to 23.2 trillion yuan. This is not the typical picture of an economy interested only in selling to the rest of the world. Nor is the story confined to merchandise. China's imports and exports of services rose 8.5 percent to 5.77 trillion yuan during the same period year-on-year. Services exports increased by 14.8 percent to 2.27 trillion yuan, while imports reached 3.5 trillion yuan. The services trade deficit narrowed by 132.66 billion yuan year-on-year. These figures suggest an economy whose international integration is becoming more sophisticated, extending well beyond factories and shipping containers. The CIIE makes these opportunities tangible. For African merchants, participation helps them replace intermediaries with direct relationships with Chinese buyers. German logistics company Jungheinrich now uses its Shanghai manufacturing base to serve 42 countries and regions. That shows access to China can generate business, investment and innovation far beyond China itself. The benefits are not reserved for multinational corporations. This year's expo has increased free exhibition space for least developed countries by 17 percent. China's extension of eligible zero-tariff treatment to goods from 53 African countries also provides a wider framework for developing countries to expand their exports. The broader context matters, too. At the 37th APEC Ministerial Meeting on Tuesday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Commerce Minister Wang Wentao called on member economies to uphold free trade, strengthen regional integration and advance cooperation in openness, innovation and sustainable development. More than 300 meetings and events have been successfully held during the APEC "China Year", producing a series of cooperation outcomes. The theme of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen in November, "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together", captures an alternative to the fragmentation now threatening global supply chains. China's pursuit of high-quality development that is innovation-driven, sustainable and inclusive means its industrial upgrading, structural adjustment, domestic demand and high-standard opening-up will continue to create cooperation opportunities and development dividends for other economies. The world has far more to gain from recognizing the "China Opportunity" than from the "China Shock" falsehood that some use to obscure it.

item.title: China's win-win philosophy is an ancient idea
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
An ancient line from Yu Xin of the Southern and Northern Dynasties (420-581) tells us: "When you reap fruits, you remember the tree; when you drink water, you remember its source." China's relations with other countries are not simply about taking what it can get. They involve a process of mutual benefit and reciprocity. This is genuine win-win cooperation, not zero-sum rivalry.
